courseTitle: Stone Age to Iron Age Britain (c. 800,000 BC–AD 43)
subtitle: Step through 10 turning points from Ice Age flint handaxes, Doggerland, Skara Brae, and Stonehenge to the Amesbury Archer, Must Farm, and Maiden Castle.

milestones.title: First Footprints & Flint Handaxes in Ice Age Britain
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why could Ice Age families walk from Europe to Britain without boats?
milestones.imageCaption: Teardrop Palaeolithic flint handaxe flaked with sharp cutting edges on both sides.
milestones.catalyst: During warm spells between giant Ice Ages, small hunter-gatherer families walked across dry land from Europe into Britain, leaving footprints in Norfolk mud at Happisburgh and chipping sharp teardrop flint handaxes.
milestones.turningPoint: Children watched elders strike flint nodules with hammerstones and helped gather dry firewood and berries near caves like Creswell Crags.
milestones.impact: Handaxes were the Swiss-Army knives of the Old Stone Age—used for slicing meat, scraping hides for warm clothes, and chopping wood!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 9000 BC): Star Carr Lake Camp & Red-Deer Antler Masks.

ks2.story: During warm spells between giant Ice Ages, small hunter-gatherer families walked across dry land from Europe into Britain, leaving footprints in Norfolk mud at Happisburgh and chipping sharp teardrop flint handaxes.
ks2.significance: Handaxes were the Swiss-Army knives of the Old Stone Age—used for slicing meat, scraping hides for warm clothes, and chopping wood!
ks2.childrenLife: Children watched elders strike flint nodules with hammerstones and helped gather dry firewood and berries near caves like Creswell Crags.
ks2.quote: “Prehistory means the vast story of human life before written records—decoded from flint, bone, and soil!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why could Ice Age families walk from Europe to Britain without boats?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Sea levels were much lower because so much water was locked inside giant ice sheets, leaving the wide grassy plain of Doggerland dry!

milestones.title: Star Carr Lake Camp & Red-Deer Antler Masks
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What were the 21 special masks found in the peat at Star Carr made from?
milestones.imageCaption: 11,000-year-old red-deer skull and antler headdress excavated from peat at Star Carr in North Yorkshire.
milestones.provenance: British Museum / Photograph by Ethan Doyle White (CC BY-SA 4.0)
milestones.catalyst: After the great ice sheets melted around 9600 BC, birch and pine forests spread across Britain. Beside an ancient lake at Star Carr in Yorkshire, Mesolithic carpenters built Britain’s oldest known wooden house and carved 21 red-deer antler masks!
milestones.turningPoint: Children learned to spot deer tracks in thick green woods, trap lake fish, and collect autumn hazelnuts to roast over campfires.
milestones.impact: Proves Stone Age Britons were not clumsy "cavemen"—they built timber platforms, paddled canoes, kept tame dogs, and held woodland ceremonies.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 6500 BC): Rising Seas Drown Doggerland — Britain Becomes an Island!.

ks2.significance: Proves Stone Age Britons were not clumsy "cavemen"—they built timber platforms, paddled canoes, kept tame dogs, and held woodland ceremonies.
ks2.childrenLife: Children learned to spot deer tracks in thick green woods, trap lake fish, and collect autumn hazelnuts to roast over campfires.
ks2.quote: “Carved eye-holes and smoothed skulls show Star Carr hunters wore deer antlers for stealthy stalking or sacred dances.”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: What were the 21 special masks found in the peat at Star Carr made from?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Real red-deer skulls and antlers with smoothed insides and holes drilled for ties!

milestones.title: Rising Seas Drown Doggerland — Britain Becomes an Island!
milestones.enquiryQuestion: What caused the grassy land bridge of Doggerland to sink beneath the North Sea around 6500 BC?
milestones.imageCaption: Map showing the sunken land bridge of Doggerland beneath today’s North Sea alongside key prehistoric sites.
milestones.provenance: The History Revision Hub Cartography Studio (Natural Earth 50m)
milestones.catalyst: For thousands of years families hunted mammoths and deer across the rolling rivers and marshes of Doggerland between Britain and Denmark. As melting glaciers poured water into the oceans, rising tides and a giant underwater landslide flooded Doggerland forever.
milestones.turningPoint: Generation by generation, coastal families watched familiar lagoons and marshes disappear beneath salty North Sea waves.
milestones.impact: Around 6500 BC Britain was cut off from continental Europe as an island—from then on, every newcomer, seed, and metal had to cross the sea by boat!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 4000 BC): First Farmers Cross the Channel With Seeds & Herds.

ks2.story: For thousands of years families hunted mammoths and deer across the rolling rivers and marshes of Doggerland between Britain and Denmark. As melting glaciers poured water into the oceans, rising tides and a giant underwater landslide flooded Doggerland forever.
ks2.significance: Around 6500 BC Britain was cut off from continental Europe as an island—from then on, every newcomer, seed, and metal had to cross the sea by boat!
ks2.childrenLife: Generation by generation, coastal families watched familiar lagoons and marshes disappear beneath salty North Sea waves.
ks2.quote: “Modern fishing trawlers in the North Sea still pull up mammoth tusks and Mesolithic bone harpoons from sunken Doggerland!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: What caused the grassy land bridge of Doggerland to sink beneath the North Sea around 6500 BC?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Melting Ice Age glaciers raised sea levels (alongside a huge tsunami wave from an underwater landslide off Norway)!

milestones.title: First Farmers Cross the Channel With Seeds & Herds
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did growing wheat and barley mean Neolithic families had to live in permanent villages?
milestones.imageCaption: Mirror-smooth Neolithic polished stone axehead ground on wet sandstone to fell forest trees.
milestones.provenance: Birmingham Museums Trust / Portable Antiquities Scheme (CC BY-SA 2.0)
milestones.catalyst: Paddling wooden boats across the Channel, newcomer farming families brought wheat and barley seeds plus tame sheep, cattle, and pigs—using tough polished stone axes to clear woodland fields and clay pots to store winter grain.
milestones.turningPoint: Children scared hungry birds off ripening wheat, milked goats and sheep, and helped coil clay pots beside the hearth.
milestones.impact: Farming began the Neolithic Revolution: instead of moving camp every season, families settled in permanent villages and shaped Britain’s farmland.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 3100 BC): Snug Stone Houses, Beds & Dressers at Skara Brae.

ks2.story: Paddling wooden boats across the Channel, newcomer farming families brought wheat and barley seeds plus tame sheep, cattle, and pigs—using tough polished stone axes to clear woodland fields and clay pots to store winter grain.
ks2.significance: Farming began the Neolithic Revolution: instead of moving camp every season, families settled in permanent villages and shaped Britain’s farmland.
ks2.childrenLife: Children scared hungry birds off ripening wheat, milked goats and sheep, and helped coil clay pots beside the hearth.
ks2.quote: “Grinding a stone axe smooth for days made a tough blade that felled oak and birch trees without shattering!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did growing wheat and barley mean Neolithic families had to live in permanent villages?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Crops took months of planting, weeding, and harvesting, and heavy pots of grain had to be stored and guarded dry all winter!

milestones.title: Snug Stone Houses, Beds & Dressers at Skara Brae
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did villagers at Skara Brae make their beds and cupboards out of flat stone slabs instead of wood?
milestones.imageCaption: Inside a 5,000-year-old Neolithic house at Skara Brae in Orkney, showing the two-shelf stone dresser and central hearth.
milestones.provenance: Photograph by S Marshall / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
milestones.catalyst: On wind-swept Mainland Orkney off northern Scotland, where few trees grew, Neolithic families built eight snug stone houses sunk into warm earth mounds—complete with stone box beds, shelved dressers, roofed passages, and indoor drains! Sand dunes hid it until a storm in 1850.
milestones.turningPoint: Tucked into cosy stone box beds padded with heather and sheepskins, Orkney children stayed warm while Atlantic gales roared outside.
milestones.impact: Older than the Egyptian pyramids, Skara Brae is Europe’s best-preserved Neolithic village and proves prehistoric homes were warm, clean, and clever.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 2500 BC): Raising Giant Sarsens & Welsh Bluestones at Stonehenge.

ks2.story: On wind-swept Mainland Orkney off northern Scotland, where few trees grew, Neolithic families built eight snug stone houses sunk into warm earth mounds—complete with stone box beds, shelved dressers, roofed passages, and indoor drains! Sand dunes hid it until a storm in 1850.
ks2.significance: Older than the Egyptian pyramids, Skara Brae is Europe’s best-preserved Neolithic village and proves prehistoric homes were warm, clean, and clever.
ks2.childrenLife: Tucked into cosy stone box beds padded with heather and sheepskins, Orkney children stayed warm while Atlantic gales roared outside.
ks2.quote: “In winter 1850 a fierce Orkney storm tore away the grass dunes and revealed eight stone homes untouched for 4,500 years!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did villagers at Skara Brae make their beds and cupboards out of flat stone slabs instead of wood?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Windy Orkney had very few tall trees for timber, whereas flat sandstone slabs split neatly right along the seashore!

milestones.title: Raising Giant Sarsens & Welsh Bluestones at Stonehenge
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Did Iron Age Celtic Druids build Stonehenge?
milestones.imageCaption: Towering sarsen trilithons and circle lintels locked together with carved stone joints on Salisbury Plain, Wiltshire.
milestones.provenance: Photograph by Diego Delso / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
milestones.catalyst: Centuries after digging Stonehenge’s circular chalk ditch with deer-antler picks (c. 3000 BC), communities hauled spotted bluestones 150 miles from Wales and dragged 25-tonne Wiltshire sarsens on wooden sledges, locking lintels on top with Lego-like mortise-and-tenon stone pegs!
milestones.turningPoint: Families walked for weeks from as far away as Scotland driving pigs and cattle to roast at midwinter gatherings at Durrington Walls!
milestones.impact: Aligned with the midwinter sunset and midsummer sunrise beside huge winter feasts at Durrington Walls, Stonehenge united communities from right across Britain.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 2300 BC): Beaker Newcomers & The Amesbury Archer Near Stonehenge.

ks2.story: Centuries after digging Stonehenge’s circular chalk ditch with deer-antler picks (c. 3000 BC), communities hauled spotted bluestones 150 miles from Wales and dragged 25-tonne Wiltshire sarsens on wooden sledges, locking lintels on top with Lego-like mortise-and-tenon stone pegs!
ks2.significance: Aligned with the midwinter sunset and midsummer sunrise beside huge winter feasts at Durrington Walls, Stonehenge united communities from right across Britain.
ks2.childrenLife: Families walked for weeks from as far away as Scotland driving pigs and cattle to roast at midwinter gatherings at Durrington Walls!
ks2.quote: “Carved stone pegs (tenons) slotted into hollowed holes (mortises) have held Stonehenge’s 7-tonne lintels steady for 4,500 years.”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Did Iron Age Celtic Druids build Stonehenge?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: No! Stonehenge was begun around 3000 BC and its giant stones stood by 2500 BC—over 2,000 years before Iron Age Druids lived!

milestones.title: Beaker Newcomers & The Amesbury Archer Near Stonehenge
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Which TWO metals did Bronze Age smiths melt together at 1,000°C to cast bronze?
milestones.imageCaption: Grave of the Amesbury Archer (c. 2300 BC) displayed at Salisbury Museum with Beaker pots, copper knives, and flint arrowheads.
milestones.provenance: Salisbury Museum / Photograph by TobyEditor (CC BY 4.0)
milestones.catalyst: Three miles from Stonehenge, archaeologists in 2002 uncovered Britain’s richest Early Bronze Age grave: a limping traveller buried with 5 Bell Beaker pots, 3 copper knives, gold hair rings, and a metalworker’s cushion stone—whose tooth enamel proved he grew up near the Alps!
milestones.turningPoint: At Great Orme in North Wales, nimble Bronze Age children squeezed into narrow rock tunnels just 30cm wide to chip green copper ore with bone picks!
milestones.impact: Marks the dawn of metalworking in Britain, soon followed by smelting Welsh copper (90%) with Cornish tin (10%) to cast tough, recyclable bronze tools.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 1900–1550 BC): The Mold Gold Cape & Dover Bronze Age Sea Boat.

ks2.story: Three miles from Stonehenge, archaeologists in 2002 uncovered Britain’s richest Early Bronze Age grave: a limping traveller buried with 5 Bell Beaker pots, 3 copper knives, gold hair rings, and a metalworker’s cushion stone—whose tooth enamel proved he grew up near the Alps!

ks2.childrenLife: At Great Orme in North Wales, nimble Bronze Age children squeezed into narrow rock tunnels just 30cm wide to chip green copper ore with bone picks!
ks2.quote: “Chemical clues from childhood drinking water stay locked inside tooth enamel—proving the Amesbury Archer grew up near the Alps!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Which TWO metals did Bronze Age smiths melt together at 1,000°C to cast bronze?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Copper (such as from Great Orme in Wales) and Tin (from Cornwall and Devon)!

milestones.title: The Mold Gold Cape & Dover Bronze Age Sea Boat
milestones.enquiryQuestion: How were the thick oak planks of the Dover Bronze Age Boat held together without iron nails?
milestones.imageCaption: The Mold Gold Cape (c. 1900–1600 BC), hammered from a single ingot of Welsh gold in Flintshire.
milestones.provenance: British Museum / Photograph by BabelStone (CC BY-SA 3.0)
milestones.catalyst: Master goldsmiths beat a single golf-ball-sized lump of Welsh gold into the shimmering Mold Gold Cape, while shipwrights at Dover stitched giant oak planks together with twisted yew branches and moss to paddle copper and tin cargos across the English Channel!
milestones.turningPoint: Coastal children watched 15-metre oak sea boats beach on Kentish shingle loaded with continental bronze axes and amber.
milestones.impact: Proves Bronze Age Britain was wealthy, artistic, and busy trading metals across the sea over 3,500 years ago.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 850 BC): Fire & Mud Freeze Everyday Life at Must Farm Stilt Village.

ks2.story: Master goldsmiths beat a single golf-ball-sized lump of Welsh gold into the shimmering Mold Gold Cape, while shipwrights at Dover stitched giant oak planks together with twisted yew branches and moss to paddle copper and tin cargos across the English Channel!
ks2.significance: Proves Bronze Age Britain was wealthy, artistic, and busy trading metals across the sea over 3,500 years ago.
ks2.childrenLife: Coastal children watched 15-metre oak sea boats beach on Kentish shingle loaded with continental bronze axes and amber.
ks2.quote: “Excavated six metres beneath a Dover street in 1992, the Dover Boat is the world’s oldest surviving sea-going wooden boat!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: How were the thick oak planks of the Dover Bronze Age Boat held together without iron nails?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Stitched tightly with twisted yew-wood bindings and sealed waterproof with moss and animal fat!

milestones.title: Fire & Mud Freeze Everyday Life at Must Farm Stilt Village
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why didn’t the wooden wheel, woven cloth, and porridge rot away beneath Must Farm?
milestones.imageCaption: 3,000-year-old Bronze Age clay pot excavated intact from waterlogged river silt at Must Farm in Cambridgeshire.
milestones.provenance: Photograph by Cmglee / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
milestones.catalyst: Near Peterborough, five wooden roundhouses stood on oak stilts above a Fenland river. When fire swept the roofs around 850 BC, every villager escaped safely—while their homes splashed into wet, oxygen-free mud that preserved Britain’s oldest wheel, fine cloth, eel traps, and bowls of porridge!
milestones.turningPoint: Children wore soft woven plant-fibre tunics, checked wicker eel traps in the river below their floor, and ate warm wheat porridge with wooden spoons.
milestones.impact: Nicknamed "Britain’s Pompeii", Must Farm reveals furniture, woven flax clothes, meals, and Mediterranean glass beads that rot away on dry land.
milestones.bridgeToNext: Next turning point (c. 800 BC – AD 43): Red-Hot Iron, Maiden Castle Hillfort & Eve of Rome.

When fire swept the roofs around 850 BC, every villager escaped safely—while their homes splashed into wet, oxygen-free mud that preserved Britain’s oldest wheel, fine cloth, eel traps, and bowls of porridge!
ks2.significance: Nicknamed "Britain’s Pompeii", Must Farm reveals furniture, woven flax clothes, meals, and Mediterranean glass beads that rot away on dry land.
ks2.childrenLife: Children wore soft woven plant-fibre tunics, checked wicker eel traps in the river below their floor, and ate warm wheat porridge with wooden spoons.
ks2.quote: “Wet, airless river silt stopped rot bacteria in their tracks—even saving wooden spoon marks inside 3,000-year-old porridge!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why didn’t the wooden wheel, woven cloth, and porridge rot away beneath Must Farm?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: They were charred by fire and sank immediately into wet, oxygen-free river mud where rot bacteria could not survive!

milestones.title: Red-Hot Iron, Maiden Castle Hillfort & Eve of Rome
milestones.enquiryQuestion: Why did iron replace bronze for everyday ploughs, axes, and swords after 800 BC?
milestones.imageCaption: Giant grass-covered chalk ramparts and defensive ditches at Maiden Castle Iron Age hillfort in Dorset.
milestones.provenance: Photograph by Hadrianus1959 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)
milestones.catalyst: Blacksmiths hammered glowing local iron into tough ploughs and swords, feeding Celtic tribes who built tall thatched roundhouses, giant multi-banked hillforts like Maiden Castle, twisted Snettisham gold torcs, and tribal coins—right until Emperor Claudius’s Roman legions invaded in AD 43!
milestones.turningPoint: Inside thatched roundhouses, children spun heavy stone rotary querns to grind flour, fed hearth fires, and practised slinging smooth river pebbles.
milestones.impact: Completes over 800,000 years of British prehistory and bridges directly into Key Stage 2 Roman Britain in AD 43!
milestones.bridgeToNext: Completes all 10 turning points in Stone Age to Iron Age Britain (c. 800,000 BC–AD 43).

ks2.story: Blacksmiths hammered glowing local iron into tough ploughs and swords, feeding Celtic tribes who built tall thatched roundhouses, giant multi-banked hillforts like Maiden Castle, twisted Snettisham gold torcs, and tribal coins—right until Emperor Claudius’s Roman legions invaded in AD 43!
ks2.significance: Completes over 800,000 years of British prehistory and bridges directly into Key Stage 2 Roman Britain in AD 43!
ks2.childrenLife: Inside thatched roundhouses, children spun heavy stone rotary querns to grind flour, fed hearth fires, and practised slinging smooth river pebbles.
ks2.quote: “Maiden Castle’s towering chalk ramparts enclosed space for 47 football pitches—guarding families, markets, and winter grain!”
ks2.detectiveQuestion: Why did iron replace bronze for everyday ploughs, axes, and swords after 800 BC?
ks2.detectiveAnswer: Iron ore was common across Britain (no rare tin needed!) and hammered red-hot iron stayed harder and sharper than cast bronze!
